newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRANCE WANTS 30 BLN FFR FROM EDF FOR 98 BUDGET - PAPER.
newsitem.headline: FRANCE WANTS 30 BLN FFR FROM EDF FOR 98 BUDGET - PAPER.

text.p: The French government has decided to use about 30 billion francs ($4.8 billion) from state-owned utility Electricite de France-Gaz de France's accounts to help cut the 1998 budget deficit, financial daily L'Agefi reported on Tuesday.

The one-time payment will come from money EdF-GdF has already provisioned for the Rhine-Rhone canal construction. The Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Lionel Jospin cancelled the canal project was cancelled for environmental reasons, the paper said without naming any sources.

The government used a one-off transfer of 37.5 billion francs from the accounts of France Telecom to help lower the 1997 deficit, and analysts have been speculating whether the government would use a similar tactic in 1998.
No one at Jospin's office was available for comment when contacted.

French governments routinely tap state-owned companies such as state bank Caisse des Depots for so-called non-fiscal budgetary receipts and the press has long been speculating that it would have to raise the amount it took in 1998.

The newspaper said the government's job in cutting the deficit would be made easier by the near 20 percent rise of the dollar against the franc this year and the automatic increase in tax receipts that would result in 1998 if the dollar maintained its gains.
The franc's weakness is expected to boost corporate profits.

Quoting an anonymous official, the paper said that given the rise in the dollar, the government planned to limit its spending to "no less than inflation and no more than gross domestic product growth", which could be slightly less restrictive than previous prime minister Alain Juppe's plans to cap the rise in constant prices.
Government sources have said previously that Jospin was aiming to limit next year's spending rise to less than two percent and perhaps as low as inflation.
The previous government, which was ousted from power in June, had planned to limit spending increases to possibly less than inflation, which is expected to be about 1.2 percent next year.
Official economic forecasts dating back to Juppe's government predict GDP growth at 2.8 percent in 1998 after 2.3 percent this year, but few private economists expect these targets to be met.
